subject: Network connectivity for ZenHealth private deployment — VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs Site-to-Site VPN

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We are moving toward a Private deployment of Redwood in our AWS account (single region for now) and need to lock down the network topology. Our infra constraints:
- We run in a restricted VPC with strict egress rules (only TLS 443 outbound to whitelisted IPs).
- We have a corporate firewall and a Palo Alto NGFW pair at the edge.
- Compliance requires that traffic to vendor endpoints minimizes internet exposure; preference is for private connectivity.

Options we are considering based on initial guidance: VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (Interface endpoints), or site-to-site VPN (IPSec) back to our on-prem/colo equipment. Can you provide Redwood's recommended pattern for:
- Least operational risk for a 1st deployment (PoC -> Prod)
- Performance/latency expectations and limits
- Any constraints around cross-account routing / transitive traffic
- TLS/mTLS support and suggested authentication model

Sam — thanks for the details and the inventory. High level: all three options are viable but tradeoffs matter depending on your security posture and expected traffic profile. Quick summary before we dive deeper on a call: 

- VPC Peering: simplest to set up for cross-VPC L3 connectivity in the same region; good for low operational overhead when both sides are in AWS accounts you control. Not transitive (can't peer across accounts through a third VPC).

- AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint): provides an ENI-based private endpoint in your VPC; traffic stays on the AWS fabric, no public IPs required on our side. Preferred when you need strong isolation and to avoid route table peering complexity. Slightly more operational overhead (endpoint ENIs, SGs) but serves well for tenant isolation and controlled exposure.

- Site-to-Site VPN: best when you need to traverse corporate network devices or when deploying Redwood on-prem/colo and you want a deterministic tunnel. Adds edge complexity (HA VPN, monitoring) and may have variable latency depending on path.

I'll loop Karthik (infrastructure architect) to sketch the recommended topology and point to a short pros/cons doc and a diagram. Can we get 30–45 minutes Tuesday 5/11 10:00–11:00 PT?

Thanks,
Soojin
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Sam / Team — thanks for the inventory and context. I pulled together a more detailed comparison tailored to ZenHealth's constraints and the typical Redwood Private deployment patterns. Key points below; I'll attach a config snippet and diagram for reference.

1) VPC Peering
- Pros: very low latency (single AWS backbone hop), simple routing when both VPCs are in accounts you control, no endpoint hours/billing.
- Cons: Not transitive; if you need to route through a transit VPC you must use Transit Gateway. Also route table bloat at scale and more manual control of SGs required. For compliance, peering exposes the full L3 between VPCs (unless you restrict via SGs), which may be broader than you want.
- When to use: small-scale deployments where Redwood components and customer workloads live in AWS and you want minimal operational overhead.

2) AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints)
- Pros: Strongly scoped (only the published service ports are exposed), traffic remains on the AWS network (no internet), easier for security teams to audit, and supports endpoint policies. Ideal when you need to offer a service endpoint to multiple accounts without exposing full VPC connectivity. No transitive routing issues since it's a direct endpoint.
- Cons: Additional per-endpoint hourly and data processing charges; ENI management in subnets and SG rules required. Slightly more complex setup for multi-AZ HA (one endpoint per AZ).
- When to use: production-grade private connectivity where security teams require minimal blast radius and per-service access control.

3) Site-to-Site VPN
- Pros: Works well if you need to cross on-prem firewall appliances or maintain corporate egress controls. Supports IPsec with BGP (dynamic routing) and can be put behind HA devices.
- Cons: Latency variability, overhead of managing keys and rotation, and potential MTU issues. Also, if you want to avoid public internet exposure entirely, you'll need AWS Direct Connect or partner private connectivity instead of standard public VPN.
- When to use: Hybrid scenarios or when customer policies mandate traffic traverses specific on-prem security tooling.

Operational recommendations for ZenHealth (suggested path):
- PoC: Start with a PrivateLink endpoint for the Redwood control plane/API surface + a single site-to-site VPN back to your office/colo for admin access and log shipping. This allows quick testing of traffic patterns while keeping production blast radius limited.
- Prod: Move to PrivateLink for data plane and API endpoints. If you need higher throughput / many services, evaluate Transit Gateway with VPC attachments or a Direct Connect + Private VIF for predictable bandwidth and lower egress variability.

Security notes:
- TLS across the wire + mTLS between your collectors and Redwood endpoints: Redwood supports certificate-based mTLS for service-to-service. We'll coordinate cert provisioning or recommend using your corporate PKI (ACME or internal CA).
- Auditability: PrivateLink + endpoint policies make it easier to satisfy SOC2 auditors because you can show per-service access controls.

Attachments:

- rdw_vpclink-vs-vpn-diagram.pdf (pdf) — topology diagram

Happy to run a short design call and then produce a one-page recommended topology that we can route to your security team.

Quick internal sync — looping Marissa to flag a couple of commercial points before we propose the final topology to ZenHealth: 

- PrivateLink has per-endpoint and data processing costs. If ZenHealth expects high egress (large batch embeddings or high token throughput), we should model unit economics and present a cost comparison (PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway vs Direct Connect).
- If they require Direct Connect / DX or a dedicated private connection for SLA reasons we need to scope a timeline + possible one-time integration fee.
- We should avoid committing to a 99.99% SLA on the first POC; propose an engineering validation window and then a dedicated capacity contract once throughput and failover testing are complete.

Action items:
- Marissa, can you prepare a brief cost estimate (ballpark) for PrivateLink per AZ and Transit Gateway + DX scenarios?
